name: probability space (Omega, F, P)
essential_semantics: The triple of sample space, sigma-algebra and probability measure is nameable, so that different random objects can be stated to live on the same space or on different ones.
canonical_example: let (Omega, F, P) be a probability space
rationale: Joint statements about several random variables presuppose a common space; without it, dependence cannot be stated at all, only assumed.

name: event as a measurable set
essential_semantics: An event is a set of outcomes closed under the Boolean operations, distinct from a proposition about parameters and from a random variable.
rationale: P(.) takes events, not truth values; systems that pass Booleans to a probability operator have lost the event/proposition distinction.

name: probability measure and its axioms
essential_semantics: A measure with total mass 1 and countable additivity, applied to events and yielding a value in [0,1].
canonical_example: P(Omega) = 1, P(A union B) = P(A) + P(B) for disjoint A, B
rationale: Normalisation and additivity are what make a probability a probability; without them any non-negative weighting looks the same.

name: random variable as an object distinct from its distribution and from its value
essential_semantics: A measurable function from the sample space to a value space; it is neither a number nor a distribution, and its identity supports dependence with other random variables.
canonical_example: X : Omega -> R with X ~ Normal(0,1)
rationale: The three-way distinction between a random variable, its distribution, and a realised value is the single most important type distinction in probabilistic modelling; collapsing any pair of them makes dependence, conditioning and pushforward inexpressible.

name: realisation / observed value of a random variable
essential_semantics: A concrete outcome value, typed as an element of the value space and distinguished from the random variable that produced it.
canonical_example: x = 1.7 is an observed value of X
rationale: The upper-case X versus lower-case x convention encodes a real type distinction that most programming representations erase.

name: distribution as a first-class object
essential_semantics: A distribution can be named, passed, compared, transformed and returned without any sampling occurring; it is not a value of the underlying type.
rationale: If Normal(0,1) evaluates to a sample rather than denoting a measure, no statement about the distribution itself can be made.

name: the 'distributed as' relation
essential_semantics: A relation between a random variable and a distribution, distinct from equality, from assignment and from approximation.
rationale: Writing X = Normal(mu, sigma) instead of X ~ Normal(mu, sigma) is a type error that silently changes a distributional claim into an identity.

name: parametric family with named parameters
essential_semantics: The family name plus the parameter tuple, with the parameterisation convention explicit (variance versus standard deviation, rate versus scale).
canonical_example: Gamma(shape = 2, rate = 3) is not Gamma(shape = 2, scale = 3)
rationale: Silent parameterisation mismatch is one of the most frequent real errors in statistical software and is pure semantic loss.

name: semantic role of a distribution parameter
essential_semantics: Parameters carry roles (location, scale, shape, rate, degrees of freedom, concentration) with associated constraints, not merely positions.
canonical_example: in Normal(mu, sigma), mu is location and sigma > 0 is scale
rationale: Roles determine constraints and unit behaviour: a location shares units with the variate, a shape parameter is dimensionless.

name: support of a distribution
essential_semantics: The set on which the distribution places mass, part of the distribution's identity and constraining admissible observations.
rationale: Observing a value outside the support makes the likelihood zero; a representation without support cannot detect impossible data.

name: probability mass function
essential_semantics: Point-mass function for a discrete distribution, summing to one over a countable support.
rationale: P(X = x) is meaningful for discrete and zero for continuous variables; a system that offers one density concept for both is wrong for at least one.

name: probability density with respect to a reference measure
essential_semantics: A density is relative to a base measure and its value is not a probability; it can exceed one and carries reciprocal units of the variate.
rationale: Treating a density value as a probability is a standing error, and the reference measure is exactly what discrete/continuous unification needs.

name: cumulative distribution function
essential_semantics: Right-continuous non-decreasing function with limits 0 and 1, defined for all distributions including mixed ones.
rationale: The CDF is the representation that works uniformly across discrete, continuous and mixed distributions.

name: quantile function / generalised inverse CDF
essential_semantics: Generalised inverse defined even when the CDF is not strictly increasing, with the convention explicit.
canonical_example: the 0.975 quantile of the standard normal is about 1.96
rationale: Interval estimates are quantile statements; ties and jumps require the generalised inverse convention to be stated.

name: expectation as an integral against a distribution
essential_semantics: E[g(X)] binds X against a specified distribution; the distribution used must be explicit, and existence is a condition, not a guarantee.
canonical_example: E[X] = integral x f_X(x) dx, undefined for Cauchy
rationale: Expectation is a binder over a distribution; ambiguity about which distribution is integrated against is a major source of error in nested-expectation formulas.

name: variance, covariance and correlation
essential_semantics: Second-moment quantities with correct types (variance non-negative, covariance matrix PSD, correlation in [-1,1]) and units (squared units for variance).
rationale: The PSD constraint on covariance matrices and the squared units of variance are both routinely violated by naive representations.

name: moments, central moments and cumulants
essential_semantics: Moments of any order with existence conditions and the raw/central/standardised distinction.
canonical_example: skewness is the third standardised moment
rationale: Method-of-moments and diagnostics depend on order and centring, which are easy to conflate.

name: moment generating and characteristic functions
essential_semantics: Transforms of a distribution with their domains of existence, the characteristic function always existing and the MGF not.
rationale: The existence gap between MGF and characteristic function is a real distinction that a lossy representation would erase.

name: joint distribution of several random variables
essential_semantics: A distribution over a product space that determines all marginals but is not determined by them.
rationale: Dependence lives only in the joint; a representation storing per-variable distributions has silently assumed independence.

name: marginal distribution and marginalisation
essential_semantics: Obtained by integrating or summing out variables, with the marginalised variable identified.
rationale: Marginalisation is the fundamental probabilistic inference operation and is a binder-eliminating transformation.

name: conditional probability given an event
essential_semantics: P(A | B) defined for P(B) > 0, with the positivity condition attached and the asymmetry of conditioning preserved.
canonical_example: P(A | B) = P(A intersect B) / P(B)
rationale: Conditioning is asymmetric and partial; both facts are frequently lost, producing the classic base-rate and inverse-probability errors.

name: conditional distribution given a random variable
essential_semantics: A distribution-valued function of the conditioning variable (a Markov kernel), not a single distribution.
canonical_example: Y | X = x ~ Normal(beta x, sigma^2)
rationale: Every regression and hierarchical model is a conditional distribution; representing it as a distribution with a parameter that happens to mention x loses the kernel structure.

name: conditioning on a sigma-algebra
essential_semantics: Conditional expectation given a sub-sigma-algebra, defined almost surely and characterised by a projection property rather than by a formula.
canonical_example: E[X | G] is G-measurable and integrates to E[X] over every G-set
rationale: This is the general form of conditioning that handles conditioning on probability-zero events; its absence caps a system's probabilistic expressiveness.

name: conditional expectation as a random variable
essential_semantics: E[Y | X] is itself a random variable (a function of X), not a number; the tower property is statable.
rationale: The random-variable nature of conditional expectation is what makes the tower property and regression functions meaningful.

name: independence
essential_semantics: A property of a collection of random variables or events with respect to a specific measure; pairwise independence is distinct from mutual independence.
canonical_example: X and Y independent means P(X in A, Y in B) = P(X in A) P(Y in B)
rationale: Independence is an assumption with consequences; if it cannot be stated it will be assumed by default, which is the worst outcome.

name: conditional independence
essential_semantics: X independent of Y given Z, a ternary relation that neither implies nor is implied by marginal independence.
rationale: Graphical models, causal inference and Markov structure are all conditional-independence statements; it is irreducibly ternary.

name: exchangeability
essential_semantics: Invariance of the joint distribution under permutation of indices, weaker than i.i.d.
canonical_example: an exchangeable sequence need not be independent
rationale: It is the correct assumption behind hierarchical models; substituting i.i.d. is a strictly stronger and often false claim.

name: i.i.d. family
essential_semantics: An indexed family that is both independent and identically distributed, with the index set explicit.
rationale: The i.i.d. assumption underwrites nearly all elementary inference; it bundles two separable assumptions that should remain separable.

name: indexed family of random variables
essential_semantics: A collection (X_i) over an index set where the index is a bound variable and the family is one object with a joint law.
rationale: Data models are families of random variables with index-dependent parameters; without indexing, only scalar toy models are expressible.

name: function whose value is a distribution (Markov kernel)
essential_semantics: A map from parameters or observations to distributions, typed as such, without collapsing to a sampled value.
rationale: This is where most probabilistic programming systems collapse a distribution into a sample; the type Distribution[T] as a return type is the discriminating capability.

name: mixture distribution
essential_semantics: A convex combination of distributions with weights summing to one, distinguished from a sum of random variables.
rationale: Mixing distributions and adding random variables are different operations with different results; the notation invites confusion.

name: hierarchical / generative model structure
essential_semantics: A sequence of conditional statements whose dependency order is explicit and acyclic, defining a joint law by composition.
rationale: Modern Bayesian modelling is hierarchical; representing only the flat joint loses the generative structure needed for inference and criticism.

name: distribution of a transformed random variable
essential_semantics: The law of g(X) as the pushforward of the law of X, defined without reference to densities.
canonical_example: if X ~ Normal(0,1) then X^2 ~ ChiSquared(1)
rationale: Arithmetic on random variables must produce a law, not a number; this is the operation that makes X + Y meaningful.

name: density transformation with Jacobian
essential_semantics: Density of a transformed variable includes the absolute Jacobian determinant and requires the transform to be a diffeomorphism.
rationale: Omitting the Jacobian is a well-known and silent source of incorrect posteriors.

name: arithmetic on random variables preserving dependence
essential_semantics: X + Y is a random variable on the same space whose law depends on the joint law, not merely on the marginals.
canonical_example: Var(X + Y) = Var X + Var Y + 2 Cov(X, Y)
rationale: Systems that implement X + Y by convolving marginals have silently assumed independence, a common and serious error.

name: stochastic process indexed by time or space
essential_semantics: A family of random variables indexed by a continuum or a discrete set, with the index set and state space distinguished.
rationale: Time-series and spatial models are processes; representing them as vectors of random variables loses the continuum index.

name: filtration / information over time
essential_semantics: An increasing family of sigma-algebras representing accumulating information, and adaptedness of a process to it.
rationale: Statements about not using future information are filtration statements; without them the constraint is only a convention.

name: Markov property
essential_semantics: Conditional independence of the future from the past given the present, stated as a property of a process.
rationale: It is the assumption that makes dynamic programming and MCMC valid; it must be assertable and checkable, not implicit.

name: martingale property
essential_semantics: E[X_{t+1} | F_t] = X_t, requiring conditional expectation with respect to a filtration.
canonical_example: a fair game's fortune is a martingale
rationale: A compact test of whether conditional expectation on sigma-algebras is genuinely supported.

name: stopping time
essential_semantics: A random time whose occurrence is determined by information available up to that time.
canonical_example: the first t with X_t > a is a stopping time
rationale: Optional stopping is a real inferential hazard (peeking at data); representing it requires the information structure.

name: modes of stochastic convergence
essential_semantics: Almost sure, in probability, in L^p and in distribution are distinct relations with a strict implication ordering.
canonical_example: convergence in probability does not imply almost sure convergence
rationale: Asymptotic statistical guarantees are stated in a specific mode; substituting one for another changes what is guaranteed.

name: laws of large numbers
essential_semantics: Convergence of sample averages with hypotheses (i.i.d., finite mean) and mode of convergence stated.
rationale: Monte Carlo validity rests on it, and its hypotheses (finite mean) are frequently violated silently.

name: central limit theorem and asymptotic normality
essential_semantics: Convergence in distribution of a normalised sum, with the normalisation and finite-variance hypothesis explicit.
canonical_example: sqrt(n)(Xbar - mu)/sigma converges in distribution to Normal(0,1)
rationale: Most frequentist intervals are CLT-based approximations; representing them as exact drops the asymptotic qualifier.

name: copula / separation of marginals from dependence
essential_semantics: Representation of a joint law as marginals plus a dependence structure on the unit cube.
rationale: It makes explicit that marginals do not determine the joint, which is the core misconception copulas exist to correct.

name: matrix- and vector-valued random variables
essential_semantics: A random variable whose value space is a matrix or vector space, with shape typing and distributional constraints (e.g. Wishart yields PSD matrices) simultaneously enforced.
canonical_example: Sigma ~ InverseWishart(nu, Psi) with Sigma symmetric positive definite
rationale: This is the hardest routine composition in applied Bayesian statistics: randomness, shape and structural constraints must all hold at once.

name: random functions and function-valued distributions
essential_semantics: A distribution over a function space (e.g. a Gaussian process) where a draw is a function, not a number.
canonical_example: f ~ GP(m, k), f(x) is then a random variable for each x
rationale: Nonparametric Bayesian methods need distributions over functions; systems limited to numeric variates cannot type them.

name: entropy and mutual information
essential_semantics: Functionals of a distribution (not of a sample) with the base of the logarithm and reference measure declared.
rationale: Differential entropy is not invariant under reparameterisation; the reference measure is genuine semantic content.

name: divergences between distributions
essential_semantics: KL, total variation, Wasserstein and similar, with asymmetry and absolute-continuity conditions explicit.
canonical_example: KL(q || p) is not KL(p || q)
rationale: Variational objectives are divergences; direction and support conditions change the optimum and are easily dropped.

name: truncation and censoring
essential_semantics: Restricting a distribution to a subset with renormalisation (truncation), versus partial observation of the value (censoring); the two are distinct.
rationale: Truncation changes the distribution, censoring changes the likelihood; conflating them yields wrong inference.

name: Bayes rule as a relation among distributions
essential_semantics: Posterior proportional to likelihood times prior, with the normalising constant and its existence acknowledged.
canonical_example: p(theta | x) = p(x | theta) p(theta) / p(x)
rationale: It is the inference rule of Bayesian statistics and requires distinguishing the four distinct distributions involved.
